title: Joining, carefully
hook: joining a tradition is serious, and each has its own way in: the Buddha tells an eager new follower to slow down
tomorrow: what does Athens have to do with Jerusalem?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: go and see. A visit, as a guest, for the whole afternoon. Today: what if the visit turns into wanting to stay?

Plenty of apps beg you to sign up: a pop-up, a discount, one tap and you're in. The Buddhist suttas keep an odd scene. Upali, a rich householder and a devoted follower of another teacher, the Jain leader Nataputta, goes to the Buddha to win a debate. He loses, gladly, and asks to become the Buddha's follower on the spot. And the Buddha, of all people, tells him to slow down.
screen: `ONE TAP AND YOU'RE IN.` → `UPALI COMES TO DEBATE.` → `THE BUDDHA SAYS: SLOW DOWN.`

segments.voice: In substance he says: make a careful investigation; that's good for a well-known man like you. Upali is even more pleased. Another teacher, he says, would have paraded my name through town on banners. He asks again, and the Buddha adds something stranger: your house has long supported the Jain monks, so keep giving to them when they come. Why would a teacher slow down his own new follower? Because in this tradition, joining is serious and has a shape. A person becomes a Buddhist lay follower by going for refuge: to the Buddha, to the Dhamma, his teaching, and to the Sangha, the community. It's said aloud, and it's meant. A rushed yes after one good debate isn't the same thing. And the word about the Jain monks shows the other side: joining one community is no excuse to slight the people who fed you before. And Upali goes for refuge a third time, eyes open. Each tradition keeps its own door. In Christianity, it's baptism. In Islam, bearing witness with the shahada. Sikhs who take initiation receive amrit. Converting to Judaism goes through a rabbinic court. Each is serious, and each is kept by its own people. So the way in isn't found on a website. You ask them.
screen: `MAKE A CAREFUL INVESTIGATION.` · `KEEP FEEDING YOUR OLD TEACHERS.` · `GOING FOR REFUGE.` · `EACH TRADITION KEEPS ITS OWN DOOR.` · then, large: `ASK THE PEOPLE WHO KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: Think of one person who belongs to a tradition you're curious about. Draft a short message asking how a person joins, and what they wish newcomers knew. Get the words right, then set the phone face down and rest with the question.
Joining: becoming part of a tradition through its own door, carefully. In Buddhism, that door is going for refuge.
Hold onto this: ask them, and listen when they tell you to slow down. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: A Buddhist lay follower goes for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, usually before a teacher or community; other traditions have their own rites of entry, kept by their own people. A newcomer asks a member or teacher how joining works there.

fork.reveal: the Buddha told Upali to investigate carefully, and to keep giving to the Jain monks his house had long supported.

original.note: Pali: I go to the Buddha for refuge, the first of the three refuges.

what a scholar hears: Majjhima Nikaya 56, the Upali Sutta: the call to investigate carefully, the banners other sects would carry, and the alms for the Nigantha monks.

chat.says: went to the zendo sunday. LOVED it. how do i officially join? is there like a form?
options: ask them. even the Buddha told an eager convert to look carefully first. each path has its own door.
just sign up online. if you loved one visit, you're already in; joining is a formality.
don't join anything. the Buddha said never to choose one teacher over another one.
chat.meaning: The Buddha told Upali to investigate carefully before going for refuge. Joining is serious, and each tradition's own people know its door.

tie.story: Upali wanted to join on the spot; the Buddha said investigate carefully, and keep feeding your old teachers.
tie.friend: Zoe can ask a member of the zendo how people join, and not rush it.
tie.you: who could you ask about a tradition you're curious about?

Upali.meaning: a wealthy householder who became a follower of the Buddha

Jain.meaning: of Jainism, an Indian tradition then led by Nataputta

shahada.meaning: the Muslim declaration of faith in one God and his Prophet

amrit.meaning: the sweetened water given at Sikh initiation

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 56, Upali Sutta (Upali, follower of Nigantha Nataputta, comes to debate; asks to become a lay follower; 'make a careful investigation'; other sects would carry banners; keep giving alms to the Niganthas; he goes for refuge)
Khuddakapatha 1, Saranagamana (the three refuges: Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Dhammaṃ…, Saṅghaṃ…)
